title: Injectable polynucleotides for the eye area: a 2026 systematic review of six trials, all in Korean and Thai cohorts
lane: Clinic and medspa incl. Korean clinics
headline: Six small studies (five split-face trials, 350 people) found short-term improvement in crow's feet with injectable polynucleotides, comparable to a polycaprolactone filler in two of them; none followed people past six months and none included deep skin.
evidenceTier: Systematic review (PROSPERO-registered), abstract read; full text not opened
fit: Clinic route (Seoul): Partial. A procedure, so fit depends on a clinician; evidence is short and from lighter skin types.
displaces: Would be a clinic add-on or replace another booster; not a home routine item.
regions: Korea, Thailand (where the trials ran); ask the clinician at the clinic
estimateNote: Prices marked EST are my guesses, not looked up.
buzzCheck: Prices not looked up; cannot judge whether price tracks evidence.
summaryPoints: Observation (abstract read): six studies, 350 participants, 80% to 100% women, Korean and Thai cohorts, Fitzpatrick III to V. 40% to 70% of treated sides improved by at least one grade on the crow's feet scale at 12 weeks.

Observation: in two trials (n=30 and n=215) polynucleotide was non-inferior to polycaprolactone fillers; in one (n=30) it beat hyaluronic acid on biophysical measures. Safety favourable; no study followed people beyond 6 months.
Inference: effect estimates are not pooled and vary by trial. Industry funding and product brands are not given in the abstract and I did not open the paper.
Limits: abstract only (full text not opened); no deep-skin data; the authors call the findings preliminary.
toneData: Fitzpatrick III to V only; East Asian cohorts
fitLine: Relevant to the Korea trip since polynucleotide boosters are common there, but the trial skin types were III to V and follow-up under six months.
timeline: Benefit seen by 12 weeks in the included trials; nothing beyond 6 months
